html:
The economic reforms that began in China in December 1978, when Deng Xiaoping and his allies won control of the Communist Party at the third plenum of its 11th Central Committee. They turned China from a poor, planned economy into the world's second largest economy within a few decades, while keeping the party in power.

After Mao's death and the Cultural Revolution, the country was poor and tired of campaigns. Deng's line was practical: "it doesn't matter whether a cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice."

The reforms came step by step, often by trying something in one place first:

  • Farms: the household responsibility system let families farm their own plots and sell their surplus. Harvests rose fast.
  • Openness: special economic zones such as Shenzhen, near Hong Kong, welcomed foreign capital and exports.
  • Business: township and village firms and then private firms grew; prices were slowly freed.
  • State firms were cut back in the 1990s, with millions of layoffs.

There were limits and costs. The party crushed the Tiananmen Square protests of 1989. Deng's tour of the south in 1992 restarted the reforms. Inequality, pollution and corruption grew. The one-child policy ran alongside.

China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and became the workshop of the world. Hundreds of millions left extreme poverty, the biggest such drop in history.
